title: BSP chief on peso situation: It’s scary
summary: With its depleting dollar reserves, the country is in a “scary” situation, even as it banks on its $98-billion buffer, Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas Governor Eli Remolona Jr. said at the…

blocks.text: November 25, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — With its depleting dollar reserves, the country is in a “scary” situation, even as it banks on its $98-billion buffer, Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) Governor Eli Remolona Jr. said at the Senate hearing on the national budget yesterday.
Remolona raised the warning after Sen. Imee Marcos pressed him on the decline in the country’s gross international reserves (GIR) to $98 billion from $113 billion.
“Isn’t it scary that our dollar reserves are getting depleted?” Marcos asked Remolona.
“It’s scary,” the BSP chief replied.

Marcos reminded Remolona of his original “safer” target of $104 billion, which he raised during a finance committee budget hearing. He maintained that the $98-billion level is still “a bit safe” because it is equivalent to six months of imports and “three times the country’s short-term debt.”
“So, exports produce the dollars, which are then spent on imports. So that’s the underlying issue,” the BSP official said.
Remolona’s response came amid lawmakers’ mounting concerns over surging inflation, which hit 7.8 percent last month from just 2.4 percent in February.
While Marcos pointed out that the BSP has already raised interest rates four times since March, Remolona said Filipinos would have to wait a year to feel the full impact of the central bank’s move.
“That’s how it is. Its effect on inflation takes about a year. And that’s the best we can do,” he said.

“Unfortunately, we have to contend with the high inflation, as you’ve indicated, and the most effective tool that any country has to slow inflation down is really the policy rate, the interest rate. From experience over 50 years, there’s no other more effective tool than the interest rate,” he added.
He did not rule out further rate hikes. “It’s already high, but so is inflation,” he said.
But for Executive Secretary Ralph Recto, the economy is expected to make a full recovery by the first or second quarter of 2027.
He attributed the current slowdown partly to a deliberate cleanup of the public works budget.

“So we expect a full recovery by the first or second quarter of next year,” Recto told reporters after the Senate’s approval of the Office of the President’s budget during plenary deliberations, when asked about the administration’s economic outlook.

Recto pushed back against claims that the government simply failed to spend on infrastructure, explaining that capital outlays for the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) were slashed from roughly P1 trillion in 2025 to P540 billion in 2026 to weed out flood control projects for review as well as curb irregularities.
“The budget of DPWH from roughly a trillion went down to P540 billion. So because of that, that is the reason for the slowdown among others of the economy with regard to the budget,” he said.
With the DPWH allocation set to rise by roughly P100 billion next year, Recto said the construction industry should see a rebound in 2027.
He added that he has yet to see the entire Senate version of the proposed 2027 budget, which he described as “growth oriented.”
He is set to meet with Budget Secretary Kim Robert de Leon tomorrow to discuss it.

Recto also dismissed US President Donald Trump’s claim that the Philippines would import 100 percent of its energy and agricultural requirements from the United States, stressing that price competitiveness remains the top priority.
“I doubt that very much that 100 percent will happen. I think 100 percent is impossible,” he said.
“What’s important is we are diversifying our sources of energy, sources of food. I think we should welcome that. I think we should also welcome having better trade with our allies,” he added.
